text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Municipalities will create few new jobs despite the extra billions of crowns they will receive from the government. Only seven of 30 municipalities plan to hire new staff, a survey by the newspaper shows.

- The Saab 9-5 is the model which is hoped to lift Saab Automobile out of the red and safeguard 8,500 jobs. The model was launched in Trollhattan, Sweden, on Monday. Saab Automobile is a 50/50 joint venture between Swedish investment company Investor and U.S. automotive group General Motors .
- The Swedish parliament will on Tuesday decide whether to allocate nine billion crowns over seven years to phase out nuclear power.
- Swedish industrial engineer Atlas Copco makes its largest acquisition ever, making a bid to buy U.S. leasing machinery group Prime Service for seven billion crowns.
- Swedish consumption is picking up to reach levels that were considered normal during the 1950s and 1960s, a report from the Retail and Wholesale Research Institute HUI shows.
- Swedish bank Swedbank wants to grow on the fund and insurance market by cooperating with Norwegian group SpareBank1Gruppen, a deal announced on Monday.

- The Swedish government will take a look at a new wealth tax to see if it can be changed to exempt all main owners of companies listed on the bourse's main A list from tax, sources told the newspaper. But Junior Finance Minister Thomas Ostros, responsible for tax issues, denied there would be a change, saying state finances needed to strengthen first.
The tax has caused several family-controlled companies to leave the bourse's main A list for the smaller O list which is exempt from tax.

- The Swedish International Development Agency (Sida) has, together with Swedfund, enlisted the services of Carlson Investment Management to set up a venture capital fund in Bolivia. Swedish state agencies will invest a total of $4.8 million in the Bolivian venture.

- Telenordia, jointly owned by British Telecom, Telenor of Denmark and Telenor of Norway, is Sweden's third-largest telephone operating firm. But it lags far behind the big two -- state-owned Telia and private phone company Tele2.

"Telenordia has only succeeded in taking three percent of the Swedish market. That isn't enough to survive," Telenordia's new chief executive Lutz Meyer-Scheel was quoted as saying. He aims to double the company's turnover.
